error_examples.summary: Any accurate accounting of actual hours worked under FLSA's principles may be used.
error_examples.rationale: The explicit scope in C0009 ('For determining hours worked under FLSA principles') and its summary omit the governing lead-in exceptions from paragraph (c)(1), which explicitly exclude airline flight crew employees governed by § 825.801 and employees returning from USERRA service under paragraph (c)(2). Consequently, C0009 impermissibly broadens the permission sentence to admit airline flight crew and USERRA situations where FLSA actual-hours accounting alone does not govern.

missing_examples.meaning: The 12 months of employment required to establish FMLA eligibility are not required to be consecutive months, subject to the break-in-service conditions that follow.
missing_examples.rationale: The substantive rule in paragraph (b) that the required 12 months of employment need not be consecutive months was entirely omitted from the draft claims.

missing_examples.meaning: Parties are permitted to use any accurate accounting of actual hours worked, provided it conforms to FLSA principles.
missing_examples.rationale: While C0009 captures the permission to use accurate FLSA accounting, it omits the governing lead-in exceptions from paragraph (c)(1) (excluding airline flight crew under § 825.801 and USERRA calculations under (c)(2)), leaving its scope overbroad and incomplete.

claim_results.rationale: Claim C0000 accurately defines the three cumulative statutory criteria required for an employee of a covered employer to be eligible under the FMLA. The summary, scope, thresholds, and alternatives faithfully capture paragraph (a) and its three subparagraphs.

source_spans.quote: (a) An eligible employee is an employee of a covered employer who:
(1) Has been employed by the employer for at least 12 months, and

(2) Has been employed for at least 1,250 hours of service during the 12-month period immediately preceding the commencement of the leave ( see § 825.801 for special hours of service requirements for airline flight crew employees), and
(3) Is employed at a worksite where 50 or more employees are employed by the employer within 75 miles of that worksite. See § 825.105(b) regarding employees who work outside the U.S.

claim_results.rationale: Claim C0001 correctly articulates the general exemption under paragraph (b)(1) that employment periods before a break in service of seven years or more need not be counted toward the 12-month requirement, subject to the exceptions in paragraph (b)(2).

source_spans.quote: (1) Subject to the exceptions provided in paragraph (b)(2) of this section, employment periods prior to a break in service of seven years or more need not be counted in determining whether the employee has been employed by the employer for at least 12 months.

claim_results.rationale: Claim C0002 correctly states the mandatory counting of employment periods preceding a break of more than seven years when the break is occasioned by USERRA service or when a written agreement exists regarding the employer's intention to rehire.

source_spans.quote: (2) Employment periods preceding a break in service of more than seven years must be counted in determining whether the employee has been employed by the employer for at least 12 months where:

(i) The employee's break in service is occasioned by the fulfillment of his or her Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act (USERRA), 38 U.S.C. 4301, et seq., covered service obligation.

(ii) A written agreement, including a collective bargaining agreement, exists concerning the employer's intention to rehire the employee after the break in service (e.g., for purposes of the employee furthering his or her education or for childrearing purposes).

claim_results.rationale: Claim C0003 accurately specifies that periods of absence necessitated by USERRA service must be counted toward the 12-month employment requirement and correctly includes the condition that it confers no greater entitlement than available under USERRA.

source_spans.quote: The period of absence from work due to or necessitated by USERRA-covered service must be also counted in determining whether the employee has been employed for at least 12 months by the employer. However, this section does not provide any greater entitlement to the employee than would be available under the USERRA; or

claim_results.rationale: Claim C0004 correctly captures the rule that being maintained on payroll for any part of a week counts as a full week of employment, including specified paid or unpaid leave periods where benefits or compensation are provided.

source_spans.quote: (3) If an employee is maintained on the payroll for any part of a week, including any periods of paid or unpaid leave (sick, vacation) during which other benefits or compensation are provided by the employer (e.g., workers' compensation, group health plan benefits, etc.), the week counts as a week of employment.

claim_results.rationale: Claim C0005 accurately states the definition deeming 52 weeks equivalent to 12 months when evaluating intermittent, occasional, or casual employment.

source_spans.quote: For purposes of determining whether intermittent/occasional/casual employment qualifies as at least 12 months, 52 weeks is deemed to be equal to 12 months.

claim_results.rationale: Claim C0006 correctly identifies the employer permission to consider employment prior to a continuous break of more than seven years.

source_spans.quote: (4) Nothing in this section prevents employers from considering employment prior to a continuous break in service of more than seven years when determining whether an employee has met the 12-month employment requirement.

claim_results.rationale: Claim C0007 correctly sets forth the mandatory uniformity requirement imposed on employers who elect to recognize employment prior to breaks in service exceeding seven years.

source_spans.quote: However, if an employer chooses to recognize such prior employment, the employer must do so uniformly, with respect to all employees with similar breaks in service.

claim_results.rationale: Claim C0008 accurately states the determination of 1,250 hours under FLSA compensable hours principles, notes the exceptions for paragraph (c)(2) and airline flight crew, and faithfully captures the primacy of actual hours worked over recordkeeping methods or agreements.

source_spans.quote: (c)(1) Except as provided in paragraph (c)(2) of this section and in § 825.801 containing the special hours of service requirement for airline flight crew employees, whether an employee has worked the minimum 1,250 hours of service is determined according to the principles established under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) for determining compensable hours of work. See 29 CFR part 785. The determining factor is the number of hours an employee has worked for the employer within the meaning of the FLSA. The determination is not limited by methods of recordkeeping, or by compensation agreements that do not accurately reflect all of the hours an employee has worked for or been in service to the employer.

claim_results.rationale: The explicit scope in C0009 ('For determining hours worked under FLSA principles') and its summary omit the governing lead-in exceptions from paragraph (c)(1), which explicitly exclude airline flight crew employees governed by § 825.801 and employees returning from USERRA service under paragraph (c)(2). Consequently, C0009 impermissibly broadens the permission sentence to admit airline flight crew and USERRA situations where FLSA actual-hours accounting alone does not govern.

source_spans.quote: (c)(1) Except as provided in paragraph (c)(2) of this section and in § 825.801 containing the special hours of service requirement for airline flight crew employees, whether an employee has worked the minimum 1,250 hours of service is determined according to the principles established under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) for determining compensable hours of work.
Any accurate accounting of actual hours worked under FLSA's principles may be used.

claim_results.rationale: Claim C0010 correctly summarizes the requirement that employees returning from USERRA-covered service must be credited with unworked hours they would have performed and have them added to actual hours worked.

source_spans.quote: (2) An employee returning from USERRA-covered service shall be credited with the hours of service that would have been performed but for the period of absence from work due to or necessitated by USERRA-covered service in determining the employee's eligibility for FMLA-qualifying leave. Accordingly, a person reemployed following USERRA-covered service has the hours that would have been worked for the employer added to any hours actually worked during the previous 12-month period to meet the hours of service requirement.

claim_results.rationale: Claim C0011 accurately reflects that an employee's pre-service work schedule can generally be used to calculate unworked hours for USERRA absences.

source_spans.quote: In order to determine the hours that would have been worked during the period of absence from work due to or necessitated by USERRA-covered service, the employee's pre-service work schedule can generally be used for calculations. See § 825.801(c) for special rules applicable to airline flight crew employees.

claim_results.rationale: Claim C0012 accurately captures the employer's burden of proof regarding hours worked when accurate records are not maintained, including for FLSA-exempt employees.

source_spans.quote: (3) In the event an employer does not maintain an accurate record of hours worked by an employee, including for employees who are exempt from FLSA's requirement that a record be kept of their hours worked (e.g., bona fide executive, administrative, and professional employees as defined in FLSA Regulations, 29 CFR part 541), the employer has the burden of showing that the employee has not worked the requisite hours.

claim_results.rationale: Claim C0013 correctly reflects the requirement that an employer must clearly demonstrate full-time teachers did not work 1,250 hours in the previous 12 months to deny FMLA eligibility.

source_spans.quote: An employer must be able to clearly demonstrate, for example, that full-time teachers ( see § 825.102 for definition) of an elementary or secondary school system, or institution of higher education, or other educational establishment or institution (who often work outside the classroom or at their homes) did not work 1,250 hours during the previous 12 months in order to claim that the teachers are not eligible for FMLA leave. See § 825.801(d) for special rules applicable to airline flight crew employees.

claim_results.rationale: Claim C0014 correctly captures the timing rule that eligibility under the 12-month and 1,250-hour tests must be determined as of the date leave commences.

source_spans.quote: (d) The determination of whether an employee meets the hours of service requirement and has been employed by the employer for a total of at least 12 months must be made as of the date the FMLA leave is to start.

claim_results.rationale: Claim C0015 faithfully conveys the rule that an employee may satisfy the 12-month requirement while on non-FMLA leave, converting subsequent qualifying leave into FMLA leave.

source_spans.quote: An employee may be on non-FMLA leave at the time he or she meets the 12-month eligibility requirement, and in that event, any portion of the leave taken for an FMLA-qualifying reason after the employee meets the eligibility requirement would be FMLA leave. See § 825.300(b) for rules governing the content of the eligibility notice given to employees.

claim_results.rationale: Claim C0016 accurately states the rule that the 50-employee within 75 miles requirement is determined at the time the employee provides notice of the need for leave.

source_spans.quote: (e) Whether 50 employees are employed within 75 miles to ascertain an employee's eligibility for FMLA benefits is determined when the employee gives notice of the need for leave.

claim_results.rationale: Claim C0017 accurately reflects the principle that once an employee is determined eligible based on notice, subsequent headcount changes do not alter eligibility for that leave notice.

source_spans.quote: Whether the leave is to be taken at one time or on an intermittent or reduced leave schedule basis, once an employee is determined eligible in response to that notice of the need for leave, the employee's eligibility is not affected by any subsequent change in the number of employees employed at or within 75 miles of the employee's worksite, for that specific notice of the need for leave.

claim_results.rationale: Claim C0018 correctly articulates the prohibition preventing employers from terminating commenced leave when headcount drops below 50.

source_spans.quote: Similarly, an employer may not terminate employee leave that has already started if the employee count drops below 50.

claim_results.rationale: Claim C0019 accurately summarizes the regulatory example and requirement to grant leave when the headcount requirement was satisfied at the time of notice even if anticipated to fall below 50 by the start of leave.

source_spans.quote: For example, if an employer employs 60 employees in August, but expects that the number of employees will drop to 40 in December, the employer must grant FMLA benefits to an otherwise eligible employee who gives notice of the need for leave in August for a period of leave to begin in December.
